findings.situation: A married head-of-household filer lived with the spouse in July and August 2025, then lived apart from September through December.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 41, Step 3 q.4: "Did you and your spouse have the same principal residence for the last 6 months of 2025? ... No. Skip question 5"; f1040 Dependents box: "you lived apart from your spouse for the last 6 months of 2025"
findings.why: The rule is satisfied only if the spouses lived apart for the whole last 6 months, so this filer should answer yes. A filer could also read 'have the same principal residence for the last 6 months' as asking whether they shared a home for that entire period, answer no, and wrongly pass the separated-spouse test. The help does not say that sharing a home at any time from July to December means yes.

findings.situation: A joint filer lived in the United States while their spouse spent most of 2025 abroad on military orders, and the filer reads the military sentence ('If you were on extended active military duty') as covering only the filer, not the spouse.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 4 q3: 'Was your main home, and your spouse's if filing a joint return, in the United States...'; p. 44: 'If you were on extended active duty outside the United States, your main home is considered to be in the United States during that duty period.'
findings.why: The question requires the spouse's home to be in the United States too, but its military sentence says only 'you'. A filer could treat the deployed spouse's time abroad as not counting and answer No, while the lines need Yes.

findings.situation: A service member abroad on orders that were for more than 90 days or for an indefinite period, but who actually served a shorter time, has to decide whether that duty was 'extended'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 44: 'Extended active duty is military duty ordered for an indefinite period or for a period of more than 90 days. Once you begin serving extended active duty, you are considered to be on extended active duty even if you don't serve more than 90 days.'
findings.why: The question uses 'extended active military duty' without this definition. An ordinary filer could judge it by the time actually served rather than by the length of the orders, and so leave out time the text counts as a home in the United States.
